r.label: Question 3

oe.title: Importance of electronegativity
groups: Chemistry you could discuss

Bonding continuum: pure covalent (equal electronegativity, e.g. H₂, Cl₂), polar covalent (small difference, e.g. H–Cl gives δ+ and δ–), ionic (large difference, e.g. NaCl, usually metal and non-metal).
Trends: electronegativity increases across a period (more protons, similar shielding) and decreases down a group (more shells, more shielding).
Structure: ionic compounds form lattices with high melting points that conduct when molten or dissolved; covalent compounds are usually molecular (low melting points) or networks (e.g. SiO₂).
Polar bonds can give polar molecules if the shape is unsymmetrical (H₂O, NH₃), causing permanent dipole–permanent dipole interactions; symmetrical molecules (CO₂, CCl₄) are non-polar.
Hydrogen bonding when H is bonded to N, O or F (large difference) explains high boiling points (H₂O, HF) and solubility in water.
Properties: like dissolves like; polar or ionic substances dissolve in water, non-polar in non-polar solvents. Polar liquids are attracted to a charged rod.
Diagrams and data to consider
Diagram of the bonding continuum with examples and electronegativity differences from the data booklet (e.g. Na 0·9, Cl 3·2).
H–Cl with δ+ and δ– labels; hydrogen bonds between water molecules (dotted lines).
Shapes of CO₂ and H₂O to show why one is polar and the other is not.

r.label: Question 5

oe.title: Group 1 and Group 4 patterns
groups: Chemistry you could discuss
Group 1 (alkali metals): all metallic bonding; low melting points that decrease down the group (weaker metallic bonds as atoms get bigger); all very reactive and form 1+ ions.
Group 4 changes down the group: C and Si are covalent networks (very high melting points), Ge is a metalloid, Sn and Pb are metallic. Bonding and structure change, so properties are less similar.
Covalent radius increases down both groups (extra shell and more shielding outweigh the extra nuclear charge).
First ionisation energy and electronegativity decrease down both groups. Group 1 values are low, so these elements lose electrons easily (strong reducing agents).
Chemical properties: Group 1 elements form ionic compounds (e.g. NaCl). Carbon and silicon form covalent compounds (CO₂ is molecular, SiO₂ a network); Sn and Pb can form ions.
Electrical conductivity: all Group 1 metals conduct; in Group 4, diamond and silicon conduct poorly, graphite and the metals Sn and Pb conduct.
Equations and diagrams to consider
Ionisation equation, e.g. Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻.
Sketch graph of melting point against atomic number for each group.
Diagrams of a covalent network (diamond) and a metallic lattice (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons).
Reaction with water, e.g. 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.

r.txt:
5.   Patterns in the Periodic Table

The Periodic Table is an arrangement of all the known elements in order of increasing atomic number. The reason why the elements are arranged as they are in the Periodic Table is to fit them all, with their widely diverse physical and chemical properties, into a logical pattern.

Periodicity is the name given to regularly-occurring similarities in physical and chemical properties of the elements.

Some Groups exhibit striking similarity between their elements, such as Group 1, and in other Groups the elements are less similar to each other, such as Group 4, but each Group has a common set of characteristics.

Adapted from Royal Society of Chemistry, Visual Elements (rsc.org)
